title: CVE-2026-86596 - s2Member <= 260927 - Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via 'item_name' IPN Parameter
text:
9.8

CVE-2026-86596
s2Member <= 260927 - Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via 'item_name' IPN Parameter

The s2Member plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution in all versions up to, and including, <= 260927 via the 'item_name' parameter parameter. This is due to insufficient sanitization in strip_php_tags_deep(), which only strips literal '<?' sequences, combined with a post-interpolation placeholder cleanup that reassembles a valid '<?php' opener after the attacker-controlled value has already been embedded in the email template. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with custom-level access and above, to execute code on the server.

title: CVE-2026-120091 - Temporal Server Kubernetes compute provider builds a client from caller-supplied configuration and runs a caller-chosen command on the Worker Service host
text:
8.7

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-120091
Temporal Server Kubernetes compute provider builds a client from caller-supplied configuration and runs a caller-chosen command on the Worker Service host

Temporal Server compiles a Worker Controller Instance module, go.temporal.io/auto-scaled-workers, into its Worker Service, and that module registers a compute provider named k8s whose function is to manage workers running in a Kubernetes cluster. The k8s provider built its Kubernetes client from the client configuration supplied in the caller's request rather than from operator configuration, and building and using that client could run a command of the caller's choosing on the Worker Service host, under the account the server process runs as. Two frontend operations reach the provider. CreateWorkerDeploymentVersion requires a namespace write role. ValidateWorkerDeploymentVersionComputeConfig is registered as a read-only namespace operation, so an authenticated caller holding only a read role in a single namespace can reach the provider through it, and that route does not require a worker deployment to already exist. Execution happens while the submitted configuration is validated, so no scaling decision, task arrival, or unusual request sequence is required. Because the Worker Service process holds the persistence credentials for every namespace in the cluster and the cluster's TLS material, the consequence reaches beyond the caller's namespace to the cluster as a whole. The provider is present in the official temporal-server binaries and container images for the affected releases. The control that keeps it unreachable is the compute provider allowlist, the dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled. On Temporal Server 1.31.0 through 1.31.2 that allowlist does not deny by default: when the setting is unset the check is skipped and every registered compute provider is permitted, k8s included, so a stock deployment of those releases is exposed. On 1.31.3 and later 1.31 releases, and on 1.32.0 and later 1.32 releases, the allowlist denies by default, and a deployment is exposed only where k8s has been added to it. The 1.30 release line does not include the Worker Controller Instance module and is unaffected. To determine whether a deployment is affected, check the following together. The deployed Temporal Server version is in an affected range. The Worker Service is running, which it is in the default service set and therefore in a stock deployment. The effective value of workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled contains k8s, or, on 1.31.0 through 1.31.2 only, is unset; check both the global value and every namespace-constrained override, because an override can add k8s for a single namespace. And authorization is configured, meaning a real authorizer and claim mapper are in place; a deployment running with no authorizer already grants every caller unrestricted access to every namespace, so it has no namespace boundary for this to cross. Deployments that use a custom authorizer should also check whether it permits ValidateWorkerDeploymentVersionComputeConfig to callers without namespace write access. The separate per-namespace dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.enabled does not gate the affected path on any affected release.

NetX Secure DTLS server allocates a session for each new source before the cookie exchange and never reclaims it, so spoofed datagrams exhaust the session pool

Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking.

Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.

Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0.

Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August.

The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are:

CVE

CVE-2026-93680
9.8 (Critical)

CVE-2026-110186

CVE-2026-110193
8.8 (High)

CVE-2026-110192
6.5 (Medium)
Yes
Getting sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials

One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP.

A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server.

Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's.

When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments."

The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable.

Upgrading to 1.13.0

Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet.

Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade:

Back up the database, the secret key and uploaded files.
If the server uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in, as Langflow's upgrade guidance describes.
Upgrade the Python package with pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0". For Docker, move to the langflowai/langflow:1.13.0 image and keep the deployment's persistent data.
If you cannot sign in after upgrading, follow the recovery steps that the same guidance links to. Do not delete or reinstall Langflow to get access back, because Langflow's documentation warns this can permanently remove your flows.

On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.

Mutipath TCP: Use and Detection

0 comment(s)

Last week, an often-ignored TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux's implementation (RFC 8684,  CVE-2026-98432)

Instead of looking at the vulnerability, I am using this diary to talk a bit about multipath TCP (MPTCP) and how you may see it used in your network.

What is MPTCP?

Traditionally, TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Connections are established between a client and server, and host IP addresses are not expected to change for a specific connection. This restriction to a specific path does not always match modern system architecture. For example, mobile devices may switch from a local WIFI network to a cellular network at any time. Having to re-establish TCP connections may break applications. At the same time, servers often have a hard time "filling" high-bandwidth links using a single TCP connection due to limits on Window Size and the sequence number range [RFC 6182]. MPTCP is supposed to solve these problems by allowing connections to be split and handed over between different IP addresses.

The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS. In this case, IPv4 connections to Apple (17.0.0.0/8) often utilize MPTCP [Apple]. MPTCP was initially used for Siri, and later for other services like Apple Music.

Two versions of MPTCP are currently defined and used: v0 and v1. At first,

MPTCP Options

The MPTCP Option (0x1e, 30) is followed by a byte containing 4 bits indicating the subtype and 4 bits indicating the version (0 or 1).

+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+
|   TCP Option   | Option Length|Subtype| Version|     Flags      |
+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+
|      30        | variable     |       | 0 or 1 |                |
+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+

MP_CAPABLE (subtype 0): Indicates MPTCP support. Both sides must include it in the TCP handshake for MPTCP support to be enabled. Each MP_CAPABLE option also carries an 8-byte key that will later be used to identify and authenticate the different sub-sessions.

MP_JOIN (subtype 1): A second TCP connection may join an initial connection using the MP_JOIN option. This connection will typically be initiated by the client, but may originate from a different IP address. The RFC does specifically allow the server to initiate the second (or additional) connection. The RFC states: "It is permissible for either host in a connection to initiate the creation of a new subflow, but it is expected that this will normally be the original connection initiator." Ports should be the same, but do not have to be. Of course, this also accounts for common firewall rules. The web server will likely listen only on port 443, and the client's firewall will reject inbound SYN packets.

DSS (Data Sequence Signal, subtype 2): Each TCP connection which is part of MPTCP maintains its own sequence numbers, and acts just like any other "normal" TCP connection. To stitch the content of multiple connections together, the DSS option is used. It maps the respective's TCP sequence numbers to the sequence numbers of the combined connection.

ADD_ADDR/REMOVE_ADDR (subtypes 3, 4): these options are somewhat similar to MP_JOIN, but instead of actually setting up an additional connection, they advertise (or remove) additional addresses or ports that can be used.

MPTCP Detection

title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
text:
Threat IntelligenceShutting the Door on the XCPE BotnetNovember 2, 2026Google Threat Intelligence Group Google Threat IntelligenceVisibility and context on the threats that matter most.Contact Us & Get a Demo Introduction 
Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).
Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. 
We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps. 
Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.
We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations. 
While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but  lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Introduction 
Mandiant responded to multiple incidents in 2026 in which threat actors hijacked enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs), a tactic known as "LLMJacking." Spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers, these intrusions impacted organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. 
Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours. Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked.Figure 1: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requestsAnalyzing the criminal ecosystem behind these frontline compromises, and building upon previous reporting on the growing underground market for LLM credentials, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has identified a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally.
As the LLMJacking ecosystem matures, we are also tracking a division of labor between threat actors establishing initial access to compromised environments and operators managing downstream monetization infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers”. LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to underground subscribers. In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space.
In this blog post, we describe the attack lifecycle observed across recent LLMJacking investigations and provide actionable detection, hardening, and remediation guidance to help organizations secure their infrastructure. 
Initial Access
While low-level resource theft has involved the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation, threat actors conducting LLMJacking bypass these front-end interfaces to target backend model resources directly. Specifically, they focus on either identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys. An example of the latter can be seen in Figure 1, where a threat actor uses an automated script to verify exposure by calling the /api/create endpoint to independently run their own models on endpoints that unsuspecting users have left publicly accessible. Leaving these services unprotected not only expands an organization's traditional attack surface, but could also introduce a significant increase in hosting costs. Introduction
As part of proactive threat monitoring, Kaspersky’s Cyber Threat Intelligence team identified a malicious campaign involving C2 agents controlled by artificial intelligence. Confirmed victims of the campaign included organizations in the education sector in several countries across Africa and Latin America. CyberStrikeAI played a key role in the post-exploitation phase. This is an open-source framework in which an LLM orchestrator on the command-and-control server plans actions, selects tools, and generates commands, while an implant executes them on compromised hosts. Using CyberStrikeAI, the attackers progressed from reconnaissance to full domain compromise.
According to our data, this is one of the first public descriptions of a compromise involving an LLM in the wild. The campaign we discovered clearly illustrates how the role of AI in attackers’ arsenals is evolving: until recently, language models were used primarily during preparatory stages – for writing phishing emails, debugging code, or searching for vulnerabilities. Now, however, they are being embedded into the very core of the attack, automating actions at every stage: payload execution, persistence on the host, discovery, lateral movement, and, finally, data collection and exfiltration. Post-exploitation – the stage that traditionally required manual work by an experienced operator – plays a particularly significant role here.
A key feature of the scheme using the CyberStrikeAI framework is that the implant ceases to be a simple tool for executing the operator’s commands. Decisions are distributed across two levels: the operator defines the task in general terms, while the model determines how to execute it – specifically, which commands to send to the host and in what sequence. Thus, the strategic planning remains with the human, while the choice of technical steps is delegated to the model, and the implant executes the model’s decisions.
To understand how this scheme works in practice, let’s examine the chain of actions taken by the attackers, as reconstructed by our analysts during the incident investigation.
Timeline of the attack

Let’s examine the timeline of the attack using an example from one incident within the detected campaign.
The first phase follows a standard approach: a human operator gains access to the victim’s infrastructure via a compromised SQL Server (version 16.0.1000), then collects basic information about the host, deploys tools, and conducts network reconnaissance. All of this activity takes nearly a day, followed by a two-week pause.
The second phase is fundamentally different. The first step involves deploying the CyberStrikeAI C2 agent, which receives commands from a server-based LLM orchestrator. During the second phase, the agent performs the following:

establishing persistence and conducting local reconnaissance within 2 minutes;
conducting domain reconnaissance over the next 5 hours;
after a brief pause of several days, moving on to the final stage – lateral movement via SMB and WMI, mass credential dumping on hosts, and database export – with the entire operation taking no more than one hour.

We’ll discuss these stages in more detail in the next section.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source, modular platform written in Go for automating penetration testing. Its key feature is combining LLM-based attack orchestration and a built-in C2 server with agents (beacons) within a single server process.

VOLTA is an AI-powered infostealer that steals personal data, then uses LLMs to assess victims’ value and rank targets for attackers.

Cisco Talos has analyzed a new Windows infostealer called VOLTA, which calls itself VOLTA-AUTODOXER. It steals the usual data, then hands the loot to a large language model that ranks what the victim is worth. Ryan Fetterman laid it out in a Talos report, after the malware turned up through the CAIRN research effort.

“There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. Every SIEM can hand its data back in one of two shapes: the original raw events, or its own parsed JSON. For analysis outside the SIEM, raw events are almost always the better choice. Why bother taking data out of a SIEM at all? For a second opinion, to share with an IR partner who has no access, or to run detection logic your SIEM doesn’t have. Prime Core has 1M detection rules across these platforms, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and LogTotal runs them against a file for free.

Six rules that apply everywhere

Export events, not summaries. Anything that ends in stats, summarize, table or an aggregation is a report, not logs.

Narrow first. Host, source, event type, time window. Count before you pull; most platforms show the number in the UI.

Use the API or CLI for anything over a few thousand events. Browser exports time out, rerun searches, or silently cap the row count.

Mind the permission boundary. API tokens often see less than your UI session: QRadar security profiles, Splunk roles, Graph scopes. When numbers don’t match, check the token first.

Pin the time zone. Use absolute windows in UTC or with an explicit offset. Relative windows (“last 24 hours”) drift if a search reruns.

Unwrap the envelope. Many APIs wrap each event: a JSON string inside CloudTrailEvent, a Records array, a result key, a CloudWatch message. Flatten to one event per line with jq before you upload.

What a SIEM can’t give you back

Original binaries. No SIEM returns Windows EVTX files; you get rendered text or JSON. For EVTX, go to the host.

Data past retention. Once it’s aged out, or moved to an archive tier that needs a restore, a normal search won’t find it.

Fields dropped at ingest. If the pipeline discarded the raw line or a field, it’s gone. Check before you promise an analyst something.

LogTotal reads syslog-style text, JSON and EVTX. Text and JSON uploads go through the sanitize step before analysis.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in your export.

Sanitize.

Review.

For everyone else, the built-in Event Log Readers group grants read access to most logs, locally and remotely, without admin rights. Add the account with net localgroup “Event Log Readers” <user> /add, then sign out and back in. A handful of channels set their own permissions; wevtutil gl <log> shows exactly who can read a given log.

Analysts, log collectors and IR partners all need event logs, and none of them should need to be local admins for it. This guide covers the least-privilege setup and the reasons “Access is denied” shows up even when you think you have rights.

Get Started For Free

Who can do what

ActionWho, by defaultRead and export most logsAdministrators (elevated) and Event Log ReadersRead the Security logAdministrators (elevated); Event Log ReadersClear the Security log or change auditingAccounts with “Manage auditing and security log” (Administrators)Change a log’s size or retentionAdministratorsRead logs from another machineSame rights as locally, plus the firewall open for remote event log access

Why admins still get “Access is denied”

User Account Control. A non-elevated session runs with a filtered token, without the Administrators group. Event Viewer and wevtutil then behave as if you were a normal user. Right-click, Run as administrator, and try again. It’s the most common cause by far.

Add an account to Event Log Readers

On one machine:

net localgroup "Event Log Readers" analyst /add

or in PowerShell:

Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Event Log Readers" -Member "CORP\analyst"

Sign out and back in; group membership is read at logon.

Across a domain, use Group Policy (Restricted Groups, or Group Policy Preferences → Local Users and Groups) to put a domain group into Event Log Readers on every machine. On domain controllers, Event Log Readers is a domain-wide built-in group, so one change covers all DCs.

Check a specific log’s permissions

wevtutil gl Security

Look at channelAccess. It’s an SDDL string, and the part that matters looks like (A;;0x1;;;S-1-5-32-573): A means allow, 0x1 means read, and S-1-5-32-573 is Event Log Readers. If a channel’s SDDL doesn’t include that SID, Event Log Readers can’t read it. You can change a channel’s access with wevtutil sl <log> /ca:<SDDL>, but it’s easy to get wrong. Prefer group membership where you can.

Remote access

Firewall. Event Viewer’s “Connect to Another Computer”, wevtutil /r: and Get-WinEvent -ComputerName use RPC. Enable the rule group on the target: Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup “Remote Event Log Management”.

PowerShell remoting (Invoke-Command) uses WinRM instead. That’s often already open where RPC isn’t.

Windows Event Forwarding. To forward the Security log, add NETWORK SERVICE to Event Log Readers on the source machines. Without it, a subscription can look healthy and deliver no Security events.

A note on uploading EVTX

Having rights to export a log doesn’t make every destination fine. LogTotal doesn’t sanitize EVTX files yet. Treat an EVTX upload as handing over the raw file, or convert it to JSON first.

When it goes wrong

title: How to Read Linux Logs Without Root (Permissions Guide)
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 02, 2026
3 min read

On most distributions, two group memberships cover nearly everything an analyst needs: adm for the text logs in /var/log on Debian and Ubuntu, and systemd-journal for the full system journal. Add the account with sudo usermod -aG adm,systemd-journal <user> and start a new login session. A few logs stay root-only by design, notably /var/log/secure and /var/log/messages on Red Hat-family systems and everything under /var/log/audit. For those, use narrowly scoped sudo, not a root shell.

Giving someone root just so they can read logs is the kind of shortcut that shows up in the next audit, or the next incident. This guide covers the least-privilege way, plus the traps that make “just add them to a group” less simple than it sounds.

Get Started For Free

LogDebian / UbuntuRHEL / Rocky / Alma/var/log/auth.log / /var/log/secureroot and admroot only/var/log/syslog / /var/log/messagesroot and admroot onlyWeb server logsroot and admroot only (the httpd log directory is locked)System journal (journalctl)root, systemd-journal, admroot, systemd-journal, wheel/var/log/audit/audit.logroot onlyroot only

Exact ownership varies with distribution and version, so check on the box itself:

idls -l /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure 2>/dev/nullgetfacl /var/log/journal 2>/dev/null

Option 1: Group membership

sudo usermod -aG adm,systemd-journal analyst

Two details matter. The -a is not optional: without it, usermod -G replaces the user’s groups instead of adding to them. And group changes only apply to new sessions. Log out and back in, or start a fresh login shell, before testing. “I added the group and it still says permission denied” is almost always an old session.

On Red Hat-family systems, adm doesn’t unlock /var/log/secure or /var/log/messages. Those files are root-only there. Use Option 2 or 3.

Option 2: Narrow sudo for root-only logs

Grant specific commands, not a shell. Create /etc/sudoers.d/log-readers with visudo -f:

%logreaders ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/ausearch, /usr/local/bin/read-secure-log

read-secure-log is a small root-owned script (mode 0755, owned by root) that does exactly one thing:

#!/bin/shexec /usr/bin/zcat -f /var/log/secure /var/log/secure-*

Why a wrapper instead of cat /var/log/secure* in sudoers? Because a * in a sudoers argument matches anything, spaces included. cat /var/log/secure /etc/shadow matches cat /var/log/secure*. A wrapper with no arguments has no such hole.

Don’t grant journalctl through sudo. It opens a pager (less), and !sh inside less gives you a root shell. For journal access, use the systemd-journal group instead.

Option 3: Group ownership that survives rotation

Setting an ACL directly works until the next rotation: sudo setfacl -m g:logreaders:r /var/log/secure. Then the file is recreated, and the ACL is gone. To make access stick, have new files created with the right group in the first place, in both places that create them:

logrotate, in the file’s stanza: create 0640 root logreaders

rsyslog, on the action that writes it: action(type=”omfile” file=”/var/log/secure” fileGroup=”logreaders” fileCreateMode=”0640″)

Test it with logrotate -f on a non-production box before rolling it out.

Containers

Don’t add analysts to the docker group just to read container logs. Membership in docker is effectively root on that host. Get container logs from your log collector or SIEM instead, or ask the platform team for read-only access there.

When it goes wrong

title: CVE-2026-112816: Critical LXD and MicroCloud Authentication Bypass Enables Cluster Takeover
text:
Canonical has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-112816, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting LXD and MicroCloud. The flaw carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to impersonate a trusted TLS client without possessing that client’s private key.

Successful exploitation can provide access to the LXD or MicroCloud API with the privileges assigned to the impersonated identity. When the trusted identity has sufficient permissions, an attacker may gain full access to the cluster, managed virtual machines, and potentially root-level access to the underlying host.

The vulnerability stems from improper validation of client certificate chains used for mutual TLS authentication. Instead of authenticating only the leaf certificate for which the client proves possession of the corresponding private key, vulnerable implementations compare every certificate supplied in the client-controlled chain against trusted certificates.

An attacker who can reach the HTTPS API and obtain the public certificate of an already trusted client can therefore append that certificate behind an attacker-controlled leaf certificate and be accepted as the trusted identity.

Canonical disclosed the issue in late October 2026 after the vulnerability was referred by the Incus project. Fixed LXD and MicroCloud releases are now available, and administrators are strongly advised to update immediately.

The flaw is especially significant in infrastructure environments because LXD manages system containers and virtual machines, while MicroCloud coordinates clustered infrastructure. Compromise of an administrative identity can therefore extend beyond a single service and provide control over workloads or the host itself.

For CVE-2026-112816 detection, security teams should prioritize identifying internet- or network-accessible LXD and MicroCloud HTTPS APIs, reviewing trusted client certificates, and correlating successful certificate-based authentication with unexpected source systems or unusual administrative operations.

SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen coverage for exploitation and post-compromise behavior across network, Linux, cloud, container, and identity telemetry.

Contact Sales

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-112816, defenders should combine vulnerable-version inventory with API access monitoring, certificate authentication telemetry, and suspicious administrative activity affecting containers, virtual machines, or cluster configuration.

CVE-2026-112816 analysis

CVE-2026-112816 is an improper certificate validation vulnerability in the HTTPS listener used by Canonical LXD and MicroCloud.

Both products can use mutual TLS to authenticate remote clients. Under normal mTLS behavior, the connecting client presents a certificate and proves ownership of the private key associated with the certificate used as the leaf of the TLS chain.

The problem arises because vulnerable LXD and MicroCloud implementations inspect more than that authenticated leaf certificate.

According to Canonical, remote API authentication logic compared all certificates presented by a client against entries in the trusted certificate store. However, TLS proves private-key possession only for the leaf certificate. Additional certificates in the presented chain are supplied by the client and do not independently prove ownership of their corresponding private keys.

This creates an authentication gap.

An attacker can generate a certificate and private key they control, use that certificate as the leaf, and append the public certificate of a trusted client elsewhere in the presented chain. The vulnerable server may find the trusted certificate and associate the connection with that trusted identity even though the attacker does not possess its private key.

An Android device manufacturer based in China supplied malware-laced devices to many brands over the years and created a botnet for ad-fraud and data exfiltration, Google researchers said Monday.See Also: 99% of Healthcare Organizations Face Known Medical IoT Vulnerabilities

The company, Videostrong Technology Co., sold criminal affiliates access to more than a million compromised devices and installed their malware, primarily on Android TV set-top boxes but also on IoT devices such as telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signage systems. The firm's pre-implanted backdoor established a botnet known as XCPE, named after a malicious Android application.

Google said it has disrupted the botnet with Japan's National Police Agency and other security organizations and banned Videostrong from making devices with preloaded Google applications.

"Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot," Google said in a blog. "As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future."

Founded in 2011, Videostrong serves nearly 100 million households in over 60 countries and regions with intelligent hardware products, according to its website. The company takes care of the entire production process, from product design to large-scale production.

Videostrong's pre-installed malware began as single-stage droppers that contained malicious payload within its own binary, Google said. From at least late 2024, it evolved into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization.

The shift followed German authorities' disruption of BadBox, another botnet campaign targeting Android TV devices, in 2024. Months later, U.S. organizations dismantled its successor, BadBox 2.0, compromised of more than 10 million uncertified Android devices.

Videostrong's malware ran with system-level privileges, enabling communication between the command-and-control server and the components responsible for loading and executing malicious code. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically came back from the firmware upon reboot.

The Chinese firm monetized the botnet to funnel malware actors' secondary modules into the infected devices from remote hosts.

"The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g. Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g. CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit)," Google said.

Videostrong was able to evade Google's security tests for hardware suppliers because its primary backdoor worked with an external loader that had native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, Google said.

The malware also wiped user consent configuration on the device and then disabled Android's built-in malware protection tool Google Play Protect.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient," Google warned. Videostrong's clients run their own diversified distribution channels. "We assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," it said.

OpenAI and Anthropic published separate October blog posts outlining how they've improved monitoring. OpenAI said it expanded its misalignment monitoring coverage by choosing a more expensive method. Anthropic said it has built a self-assessment approach that judges entire conversations.
But while these methods have improved both labs' ability to catch misbehavior in their models and agents, both companies said serious limitations remain, including inherited blind spots, difficulty recognizing emerging harms and the potential to send false alarms.
Each company said that monitoring frontier model behavior, especially after the Hugging Face breach, has become more important.
OpenAI said in a Thursday blog post that monitoring frontier model alignment is a failsafe for when safeguards fail.
"While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase," the company said.
To understand how it can find model misalignment, OpenAI said it replayed the problematic behaviors its agents exhibited during the Hugging Face breach. The idea was to learn just how an expanded and improved monitoring system could have prevented the hack. OpenAI said that had its expanded monitoring system been in place, it would have detected the Hugging Face attack much earlier, more than 30 hours before the breach.
In an Oct. 16 blog post, Anthropic said its self-assessment techniques adds a hidden safety step that users never see. Monitor models add a note at the end of the conversation asking whether anything between the agent and user is harmful, and Claude models answer yes or no. If the model flags something, it will report what the harm could be, whether it refused and its urgency. Anthropic collects this report at the end of the day and sends it to human investigators.
Self-assessment caught 78% of conversations flagged as potentially harmful with a 1% false-positive rate.
Anthropic said its approach is more affordable than other techniques because Claude doesn't need have another model to read the entire conversation again. The company said it's already seeing this approach improve as the models Anthropic releases improve, showing that self-assessment scales similarly.
"We expect self-assessment to improve as models do. This matters because oversight of how models are used becomes more important as they grow more capable," Anthropic said.

Steve Orrin, federal CTO, Intel

Preparing for post-quantum cryptography will force CIOs to coordinate work across applications, infrastructure, vendors and operational technology. Steve Orrin, federal chief technology officer at Intel, says organizations should begin by finding where cryptography is used, then prioritize systems and data according to their business importance and the length of time they need protection.See Also: Live Webinar | Go From Awareness to Action in the Post-Quantum Era

The risk extends beyond data that could be intercepted and decrypted in the future. Digital signatures and other trust relationships also could be affected, Orrin said. Because a migration may involve connected devices and systems that are difficult to upgrade, organizations need to plan before quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptography are available - a point in the future that researchers describe as Q-Day.

"You can't secure, you can't fix what you don't know," Orrin said.

Orrin recommends combining cryptographic discovery with existing asset and financial records. IT teams can identify the technology they manage, while finance can help reveal the services and vendors the organization pays for. The inventory should cover more than laptops, servers and cloud services. It should document everything including printers, badge readers, cameras, industrial equipment and third-party services that may also use cryptography.

Once organizations understand what they have, they can rank systems by the confidentiality and integrity they need to preserve. Data such as trade secrets, personal information and regulated records may need protection for many years. Digital signatures and financial ledgers may need to remain trustworthy over the life of a transaction or record. Orrin advises CIOs to focus first on high-value systems and long-lived data, then build a phased plan around business priorities and available budgets.

In this video interview with ISMG, Orrin discussed:

Why post-quantum risk includes both encrypted data and digital trust relationships;

How CIOs can map cryptography across IT, operational technology and vendors;

What to prioritize in the first 90 days, and how to test migrations in stages.

Orrin leads solution architecture, strategy and technology engagements at Intel. He has held Intel leadership and architecture roles focused on identity, anti-malware, HTML5 security, cloud and virtualization security. He was previously CSO of Sarvega and CTO of Sanctum and SynData Technologies.

The bureau on Saturday linked the Oct. 29 heist - the largest crypto theft on record - to the North Korean hacking group dubbed TraderTraitor and published an alert urging crypto services to block transactions linked to hundreds of attacker-controlled addresses. The attribution comes as customers pull billions of dollars from the world's largest crypto exchange (see: North Korea Suspected in $6.3B Binance Hack).

"The main challenge is in the steps between translating detection into action," Jenny Jun, a Georgia Institute of Technology academic who studies North Korean hacking. Attributing a crypto theft to a nation-state matters less than in other cyber incidents because the theft itself spur action, Jun said.
Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, which was among the first firms to link the theft to North Korea, told ISMG the FBI's call still matters because it "puts the U.S. government behind the attribution."

"Exchanges, OTC desks and stablecoin issuers now have a clear list of addresses to block and the cover to act on it," he said. "When funds move in minutes, that's what gets money frozen instead of cashed out."

The FBI alert, issued alongside the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, names 608 Ethereum addresses, 19 bitcoin addresses and one Solana address. It asks THORChain node operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to refuse transactions "with or derived from" them.

The bureau said the hackers have converted most of the stolen funds into ether and expects them to keep moving it through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

THORChain, a swap protocol that moved a large share of North Korea's $1.5 billion Bybit haul in 2025, has not committed to acting on the FBI's request. Co-founder Chad Barraford wrote on X that node operators have "zero information that isn't already public." Co-founder JP Thor wrote on X that if node operators took the protocol offline, "the experiment is over."

Stablecoin issuers moved to freeze funds faster than they did after the Bybit hack, Jun said - but stopping ether and bitcoin held directly by the hackers is harder as many of the services involved are DeFi platforms built to spread out decision-making.

Bringing those platforms on board takes consensus-building and sometimes structural changes, which Jun said typically would occur "in between hacks, not during an ongoing crisis."

Binance, which restarted withdrawals Sunday after a freeze of more than two days, said in a post on X that customers pulled a net $3.64 billion in the first nine and a half hours, about 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets. title: Quick web security check: can another site put your app in an iframe?If so, a page can hide your signed-in app under a fake button (clickjacking).Check: curl -sI your live URL. Look for CSP frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options.Fix: frame-ancestors 'self' (or 'none'), plus X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN or DENY for older browsers. It must be a response header; frame-ancestors in a <meta> tag is ignored.https://abbilabs.xyz/tips/can-your-app-be-framed-clickjacking #clickjacking #websecurity #infosec #webdev #AppSec #CSP #security
text: 2026-11-03 · Daily security tipsCan another site load your app inside an iframe?Clickjacking works like this: someone loads your real app, where the user is already signed in, in an invisible iframe on their own page and places a fake button over one of yours. The user thinks they clicked theirs. They actually clicked delete, confirm or change email in your app.Check: run curl -sI https://yoursite.com and look for a Content-Security-Policy header with frame-ancestors, or an X-Frame-Options header. If neither is there, any site can frame your pages.Fix: send Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' (or 'none' if you never embed your own pages), plus X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN or DENY for older browsers. Set them in vercel.json, netlify.toml, _headers or your framework's headers config.If you embed your app somewhere on purpose, list that exact origin instead of dropping the header.

title: What we built: October 2026
text:
TL;DR

This is a monthly recap of everything our product team shipped in the last 30 days
Questions? Reach out to your Expel contact, or if you don’t have one, connect with us here
October brings two new Microsoft Entra ID threat hunts and a more accurate Alert Analysis dashboard

Live this month
Alert Analysis dashboard (AAD) metrics updates
What it covers: We changed how the Alert Analysis dashboard calculates and reports metrics. Three things are different:

A standardized metrics foundation: The AAD now pulls some information from a new, standardized source, so Expel Alert counts use one consistent definition. Users may still find inconsistencies as we continue to work on this, and are encouraged to reach out to customer success with questions. 
Date ranges up to 15 months: That lines up with Workbench’s standard data retention period. If your org has extended retention, your alert and investigation data is still kept for your configured period. The AAD charts cover the most recent 15 months.
Events Ingested for webhook-connected integrations: Some integrations, like Zscaler, send data to Expel over a webhook. The AAD used to show no Events Ingested for them; now it does.

Why you should care: Your counts are more accurate, you can look back further, and integrations that used to show nothing now show activity.
The counts for Events Ingested depends on how the integration is connected to Expel:

API-connected integrations: Expel pulls data from the vendor, and the AAD counts each event.
Webhook-connected integrations: The vendor sends events in batches, and one batch can hold hundreds of events. The AAD counts each batch, not each event inside it.

That means Events Ingested for a webhook-connected integration can be much lower on the AAD than on the Security Devices page, but that doesn’t mean data is missing. Every event in every batch is unpacked and analyzed by our detections, and the Security Devices page reports those individual events. For individual event volume, open the integration on the Security Devices page and check Raw Events (last 30 days). For longer periods, like a full quarter, your customer success manager can pull the totals.

New threat hunts
These two hunts are live on the hunt catalog page in Workbench for signed-in customers with threat hunting.
1. Microsoft Entra ID North Korean IT worker fraud artifacts login hunt
What it covers: North Korea has placed fraudulent IT workers inside companies around the world. Past incidents show the same infrastructure again and again. This hunt reviews Entra ID login data tied to known VPNs and proxies, plus endpoint traffic artifacts like KVM and VDI tunnel traffic. It groups those signals around specific login applications to surface patterns, making it easier to detect.
2. Microsoft Entra ID suspicious multiple VPN usage
What it covers: Corporate VPN use is normal, and some orgs allow personal VPNs, too. But one user on more than two VPNs in a short window is unusual. This hunt reviews enriched Entra ID authentications for users showing multiple VPNs over a given timeframe.
Why you should care: Both hunts focus on identity, where attackers and fraudulent insiders blend in with normal sign-ins. Three or more VPNs for one user can point to automated post-exploit activity, and IT worker fraud often hides behind the same kind of infrastructure. Our threat hunters get a starting point for sorting the expected from the suspicious.

Hackers have again taken aim at supermarkets in Europe.See Also: Prioritize Preparation, Basics and Transparency, Experts Urge IRISSCON Attendees

For the second time in three weeks, hackers remotely accessed refrigeration systems and set them to defrost, resulting in spoiled food and some affected stores remaining closed.

Dozens of retailers appear to have been affected across seven countries: Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

"There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees" Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters when it visited the store Monday. She said the attack appeared to begin at 2 a.m. local time but wasn't noticed until hours later.

In some cases, managers said they received emailed alerts of rising refrigerator and freezer temperatures and rushed to the stores to try to save stock, including transferring it to refrigerated trucks.

The attacks, launched overnight Sunday into the early hours of Monday, follow mid-October hack attacks with identical timing that affected hundreds of supermarkets across France, resulting in food spoilage and in some cases fires. The Paris prosecutor's office has launched a criminal investigation (see: Hackers Attack French Supermarket Freezers Causing Food Loss).

France's Computer Emergency Response Team said those incidents involved the targeting of Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM controllers, and Copeland and Dixell xweb controllers. The Sunday attacks involved hackers, at least in some cases, targeting the same types of equipment.

The European food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, characterized the repeat targeting of grocery stores by hackers as being "a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers' confidence in it," reported the Guardian.

7 Countries Affected

In the latest attacks, Belgian grocery store operator Delhaize said about 40 of its stores were affected. Also affected were 15 independently owned Carrefour stores, around five Spar stores, five stores operated by discount chain Colruyt and an Ikea store in the western city of Mons.

At least some of those affected stores use systems provided by Belgian refrigeration supplier Sabcobel. "We started mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans, CEO of Sabcobel, told Belgian newspaper Le Soir. "We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid."

Moelans told the Belga news agency that it's been attempting to lock down all of the refrigeration units it manages for stores since the French attacks several weeks ago, but said the process has been complicated by physical modifications needing to be made to the units.

"That requires investment. The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," he said.

Belgian authorities have opened a criminal investigation into the attacks.

At least 17 Dutch firms have been affected, with Danish manufacturer Danfoss telling Dutch public radio broadcaster NOS that the victims were all butcher shops and smaller, neighborhood stores with cooling systems.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that in the wake of the mid-October attacks, the company issued an urgent alert on Oct. 13 to all customers, warning them to ensure the devices weren't publicly exposed to the internet, especially because they contain a default password. Residents of Kyiv take shelter during a Dec. 29, 2023, missile attack by Russia. (Image: Kyiv City State Administration/CC BY 4.0)

Early alert smartphone apps in Ukraine and then Russia were hacked to broadcast fake information as part of apparent psychological operations.See Also: OnDemand | How Okta and CrowdStrike Share Signals to Enforce Protection Against Cross-Domain Attacks
The Ukrainian government-sponsored Air Alert app on Sunday began warning residents of immediate nuclear and chemical threats, as well as street fighting. Hours later, after suffering an apparently retaliatory response, authorities in Russia reported that their own early warning app was hacked and broadcasting fake alerts.
The first disruptions emerged late Sunday, local time in Ukraine, when Kyiv Independent reported that its "journalists on the ground received notifications on their phones from the officially supported Air Alert app" that appeared to be bogus.
The false Air Alert alerts included messages written in Russian. According to local press reports, one read: "Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is on its way." Oreshnik refers to a Russian "hazel tree" intermediate-range ballistic missile designed to reach speeds exceeding Mach 10. Ukraine reportedly has no ability to intercept such missiles.
Other alerts referred to imminent chemical attacks as well as urban warfare being underway.
"Hacking a government warning app is a really good - and very unsettling for the general populace - part of a psyops operation, and of course timing is everything. This has been part of a psyops toolkit and can achieve disruption and undermine the confidence in the government - exactly what a psyop is supposed to do," said cybersecurity expert Ian Thornton-Trump, CISO at Inversion6.
Moscow has long used information operations designed to garner news headlines, unsettle Ukrainians and undercut trust in their leadership. Previous efforts have included distributed-denial-of-service attacks launched by Kremlin-funded "hacktivist" groups as well as claimed intrusions involving industrial networks (see: Malware Attacks and Disinformation Campaigns Target Ukraine).
What's unusual about this episode is the degree to which it appears to sport Moscow's fingerprints, said Don Smith, vice president of threat intelligence for the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, in an emailed statement. "Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia," he said.
Ukraine Temporarily Shuts Down App
Authorities in Ukraine quickly dismissed the fake alerts, urging residents to temporarily only pay attention to other official sources of information, including local public address systems, and to avoid clicking any links disseminated through the Air Alert app.
"Attention: The Air Alert app has likely been compromised. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" Ukraine's Air Force said in a post to its Telegram channel, Sunday evening local time.
Regional authorities disseminated similar messages.
"Currently, the situation in the oblast is calm. Reports indicate a cyberattack on the notification app," Svitlana Onyshchuk, governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk region, said in a Telegram post.
The team behind the Air Alert app, which is developed by Ukraine's Digital Transformation Ministry and security firm Ajax System, confirmed the hack attack.

title: Syrian Man Sentenced for Wide-Ranging Hacking Conspiracy Conducted on Behalf of the Bashar Al Assad Regime
text:
Ahmad Umar Agha (also known as Th3Pr0) had spent more than a decade as a fugitive for targeting of Western media entities, businesses, NGOs, and U.S. and allied government entities
October 29 – Today a federal district court in the Eastern District of Virginia sentenced Ahmad Umar Agha to 42 months in prison for his central role in an expansive hacking conspiracy organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad’s inner circle, including the commander of Syria’s General Intelligence Directorate, from as early as Aug. 24, 2011, to Jan. 31, 2014.
To spread the former Syrian government’s propaganda, Agha hacked approximately 47 Western media entities, businesses, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and U.S. and allied government entities. The hacking conspiracy penalized the free press for reporting on the former Syrian government’s atrocities during the Arab Spring and subsequent Syrian Civil War; used information warfare tactics to cause fear and confusion among Syrian government opponents; collected intelligence for the former Syrian government; and attempted to cause mutiny or refusal of duty by members of the military of the United States. In one instance, Agha’s actions caused a flash crash in the U.S. stock market, resulting in a temporary $136 billion loss in the value of stocks making up the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
“Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad’s regime to silence reporting on the regime’s atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “His attacks on our networks and institutions, including one that temporarily erased $136 billion from U.S. investors, constitute an assault on the free press and our national and economic security. Today’s sentence should serve as a reminder of the National Security Division’s long memory in pursuit of state-sponsored hackers such as Agha.”
“This case emphasizes the grave threat posed by cyber criminals and especially those serving regimes hostile to the United States,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani K. title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
text:
Vittoria Elliott reports:
sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”

title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
text:
A shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin. Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersView image in fullscreenA shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin. Photograph: Natalia Campos/Reuters ExplainerWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives

Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F).The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean? The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia.It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software.Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, dispose of spoiled food. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAThis is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control. Who is doing it?No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat. “The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos. The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea is believed to have been behind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame.Western intelligence chiefs say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months.View image in fullscreenA worker at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden disposes of spoiled food. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ShutterstockDiscerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”.How is it possible?The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates.  Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read moreNick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to […]

# Over 1,000 GitLab Servers Hit by Active RCE Attacks

The wire is full of boring breaches today. Stolen cards. Leaked databases. None of it compares to the story that actually matters. It isn't about code. It's about fear. In Russia and Ukraine, hackers have hijacked emergency alert apps. These are the tools people use to know if they need to run into a basement now. The attackers push fake warnings about nuclear and chemical strikes.

When the app meant to save your life starts lying, its value hits zero; for us running small shops, it is a hard look at how fragile "trusted" channels really are. We worry about email spam. We barely ask what happens when a critical alert tool gets flipped by someone else, and if you have tied business continuity to one unverified app, you aren't buying safety. You are outsourcing your panic.

Then there is the math. Over 1,000 GitLab servers are under active remote code execution attacks right now; for big companies, that is a ticket for the SOC team. For a ten-person shop that self-hosts to save on SaaS fees, it could be fatal. The argument for self-hosting is always simple: keep your data on your own iron, avoid per-user costs, have total control. That is the claim. Reality? Most small firms don't have control. They have a server they forgot to patch in July.

When RCE hits over a thousand servers, your source code and SSH keys become public property. Some people think a VPN or firewall fixes this. It doesn't. If you expose the instance for webhooks, the door is open. An attacker with a foothold from phishing can pivot straight through there; the "savings" are an illusion if you aren't paying someone dedicated to updates. I would rather pay a vendor monthly than spend a weekend trying to restore a backup that might not work anyway.

This exposes the cost gap. Enterprises have budgets for scanners and automated patch pipelines. Small firms have Dave. Dave handles payroll, the office printer, and security. The enterprise deploys patches in hours. Dave does it between client calls.

The real bleeding is in the supply chain. Amadeus has been hit. This isn't just a vendor breach. It is a systemic failure that forces airlines like Qantas to scrub their booking systems for holes, and reports say 38 months of airline data were exposed. The second-order effect hits passengers hardest. You didn't get hacked. Your airline was just a customer of Amadeus. But your passport and credit card are now in a leak file because a middleware provider failed. This mirrors the MoveIT disasters from years ago; the victim isn't the owner of the vulnerable software. It is everyone whose data flowed through it.

The difference here is time, and 38 months is a massive window for attackers to build profiles on high-value travelers. We have seen this before with SolarWinds and managed service providers. We keep trusting "specialized" providers to be secure vaults, only to find they left the back door open. Today's break in that pattern is the volume. Amadeus isn't just a tool. It is the nervous system for global travel.

Keep an eye on state-sponsored noise too; north Korea's TraderTraitor group is still dominating headlines after stealing $6.3 billion from Binance. The FBI has flagged over 600 addresses tied to the heist. Your ten-person shop isn't a target for nation-state crypto theft. But these groups use the same entry vectors as common criminals: leaked credentials and unpatched edge devices.

Public sector leaks are massive too. Florida's Department of Education confirms a breach affecting potentially 4.9 million people. Japan's So-net has put over 2.6 million records at risk. Wagyu Confirms Data Leak Exposing Monero Transactions and Customer IP Addresses

Wagyu, a cryptocurrency swap service specializing in Monero transactions, confirmed a data leak involving customer transaction records on October 28, 2026. The incident followed an extortion claim by the WhiteArmor group, which reportedly demanded $5 million in connection with the stolen information. The group listed Wagyu on its data leak site, and transaction records attributed to the service subsequently circulated online.The WhiteArmor group reportedly obtained Wagyu transaction records covering July 18 to October 26, 2026. The exposed information contained customer IP addresses collected through the service's website and stored alongside transaction details. These records could link public Bitcoin deposits to Monero receiving addresses and customer IP addresses. The firm verified the figures within the supplied records but could not independently confirm their origin or authenticity. The number of affected individuals has not been confirmed.Wagyu acknowledged the data leak through its PerpetualCow social media account. The company reported that its swap services remained operational and that no customer funds had been lost. Affected users should remain cautious of phishing messages referencing previous transactions, refund offers, or account verification requests. Users should verify communications through official channels, avoid sharing wallet recovery phrases or private keys, and consider using new Monero receiving subaddresses for future transactions to reduce further exposure.

title: Mobile Carriers Store Call Logs for Years, Raising Privacy RisksMillions of Americans had their personal communication logs exposed in a massive AT&T data breach, revealing sensitive information like phone numbers, call counts, and location data for nearly two years. This alarming breach puts 109 million people at risk of compromised privacy.https://osintsights.com/mobile-carriers-store-call-logs-for-years-raising-privacy-risks?utm_source=mastodon&utm_medium=social#DataBreach #Telecommunications #CallLogs #Att #EmergingThreats
text:
109 million people (nearly a third of Americans) suffered a massive data breach in April 2024 that exposed their AT&T communication logs.

AT&T breach: scale, timing, and contents
In April 2024, AT&T disclosed a breach that exposed communication logs for roughly 109 million people. The exposed records covered phone numbers, counts of calls and texts, call durations, and location data from May–October 2022 and January 2023 — roughly two years before the breach was disclosed. AT&T said the records did not contain call content, customer names, or Social Security numbers.

Inside call logs: SIP messages and CDRs
Two technical record types are central to what carriers store and what was exposed. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) messages manage the start and stop of calls and texts and are used mainly to troubleshoot dropped calls and failed texts. Call Detail Records (CDRs) summarize each call, text, and data session: who was involved, when it happened, for how long, and often which cell site a phone used. Carriers use CDRs for billing and to settle roaming charges. Even without call content or names, these records can reveal intimate details — closest relationships, home and workplace locations, daily routines, and medical or legal consultations when correlated with other information.

The source lays out three structural reasons call logs are easy to steal. First, carriers retain this data for long periods. While privacy policies commonly promise retention “as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes” stated, carriers told the FCC chair in 2022 that geolocation data can be kept for as long as five years. Second, the repositories of that data are concentrated and therefore high-value targets: the AT&T breach was one of several incidents tied to credential theft on Snowflake, a cloud data platform used by multiple large companies. Third, retained logs have commercial and operational buyers: they are used to build behavioral profiles sold to ad networks and data brokers and, in some cases, are handed to government actors. The reporting also notes that a campaign known as Salt Typhoon, described as China-linked, reportedly compromised every major U.S. carrier, illustrating the geopolitical dimension of the risk.

Cape’s deletion model and the Trail of Bits attestation
Cape, a carrier that markets itself on privacy, advertises a different approach: minimal collection and short retention windows. Cape says it deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates network identifiers to hinder tracking, and runs its own mobile core so it can control log deletion. Cape describes specific retention windows: SIP messages kept for 14 days to debug network issues, internal CDRs deleted after one day, daily totals (counts of calls, SMS, MMS, and data per subscriber) retained up to 60 days for billing and spam prevention, and partner-sent CDRs held 30 days to allow billing disputes.
To back those claims, Cape hired Trail of Bits for an audit in May and July 2026. Trail of Bits reported finding no evidence of violations of the two claims it evaluated: that CDR files are being deleted within Cape’s retention policy, and that Cape does not extract or retain data from CDRs about individual consumer customers except for daily totals, which are retained for no more than 60 days.

What this means for journalists, security teams, and end users

Journalists and executives: The source explicitly names journalists and executives among those who should treat carrier retention policies as part of their threat models. Call metadata can reveal communications with sources or advisors even when content is not recorded.

Blockchain analytics company Chainalysis has announced falling victim to an AI-driven cyberattack that resulted in a data breach.

“This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools,” the company said.

The incident, it pointed out, is not related to the recent $6.36 billion Binance heist that was blamed on North Korean hackers.

According to Chainalysis, the attack did not result in the compromise of investigation content, transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, or other credentials and secrets.

“Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users,” Chainalysis said.

The company continues to investigate the full scope of the data breach and has not disclosed how many individuals were potentially affected.

“Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems,” it said.

Chainalysis noted that it has observed an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks, as many other tech platforms have been hit in recent weeks.

The company has been working with external cybersecurity experts and LLMs to review its security posture and strengthen it against these evolving threats.

Because names and email addresses were compromised, it recommends that users watch for unexpected authentication prompts and password reset requests, and make sure they have MFA enabled.

Léon XIV en Amérique latine : héritages pontificaux, recompositions du catholicisme et enjeux géopolitiques

François Mabille

Chercheur associé à l’IRIS, directeur de l’Observatoire géopolitique du religieux

Du 6 au 17 novembre 2026, le pape Léon XIV effectuera un voyage en Uruguay, en Argentine et au Pérou, premier grand déplacement latino-américain d’un pontife dont la trajectoire personnelle est profondément liée à cette région du monde, mais dont l’élection, en mai 2025, avait également constitué une nouveauté dans l’histoire de la papauté puisque, pour la première fois, un religieux né aux États-Unis et ayant longtemps exercé son ministère au Pérou accédait au siège de Pierre. Ce déplacement présente plusieurs caractéristiques qui dépassent son importance pastorale immédiate, tant il intervient à un moment de recomposition du paysage religieux latino-américain, de transformation des rapports entre les Églises et les États, mais également d’interrogations sur l’orientation d’un pontificat dont les premières interventions ont confirmé plusieurs héritages de François sans que soit encore complètement précisée la manière dont Léon XIV entend inscrire ces orientations dans le gouvernement de l’Église universelle.

L’analyse du voyage de Léon XIV suppose donc de le replacer dans cette histoire longue, en revenant sur les orientations successivement données à la présence pontificale par Jean-Paul II, Benoît XVI et François, avant d’examiner les enjeux propres à son déplacement et les contextes politiques et religieux des trois pays visités, dont les différences sont suffisamment importantes pour permettre d’observer plusieurs modalités contemporaines de relations entre catholicisme, démocratie et pouvoir politique.

Israël : que révèle le résultat des élections législatives ?
