Didier Billion

Conseiller scientifique, responsable du Programme Moyen-Orient/Afrique du Nord de l’IRIS

Des résultats qui déjouent les pronostics

Premier constat, le taux de participation s’élève à près de 78 %, montrant que les citoyens israéliens ont considéré déterminant l’enjeu de cette consultation. Les Palestiniens d’Israël ont pour leur part voté à près de 80 %, exprimant un rejet total de la politique de Benyamin Netanyahou, Premier ministre sortant.

Le système électoral à la proportionnelle quasi intégrale montre une nouvelle fois la difficulté à parvenir à une claire majorité sans recourir à des coalitions où, traditionnellement, les négociations secrètes sont la règle, accompagnées de leurs lots de reniements, de trahisons et de renversements d’alliances.

Mais, au-delà des paramètres liés aux règles du système électoral à proprement parler, les résultats de ces élections sont avant tout l’expression des divisions qui taraudent la société israélienne sur les enjeux de politique intérieure. Les scénarios les plus divers sont donc envisageables dans les jours et les semaines à venir et il serait vain de faire des pronostics un tant soit peu tangibles dans le cadre de cet article.

Les résultats officiellement proclamés montrent que la coalition menée par Benyamin Netanyahou, composée de cinq partis, arrive en tête avec 53 sièges de députés élus, sur 120 que comporte la Knesset, le parlement israélien ; celle de l’opposition regroupée autour de Gadi Eisenkot, composée de quatre partis, gagne 48 sièges, et enfin les deux listes arabes, 19 sièges. La majorité absolue nécessitant 61 députés, c’est donc maintenant que commencent les tractations pour tenter de trouver la formule de la composition du futur gouvernement.

Plusieurs remarques peuvent à ce stade être formulées.

Bien que connaissant une sensible réduction du nombre de ses députés – la coalition majoritaire sortante en possédait 64 –, il n’en demeure pas moins que le bloc dirigé par Netanyahou ne s’écroule pas, en dépit des accusations de toutes sortes dont il a été la cible durant toute la campagne électorale : corruption, entorse aux principes démocratiques notamment incarnée par son projet de réforme judiciaire visant à mettre au pas la Cour Suprême et surtout sa responsabilité de n’avoir pas su prévenir le 7-Octobre, voire pire, avoir été mis au courant des préparatifs du Hamas et n’en avoir pas averti les services de sécurité concernés. Malgré ces accusations, une partie significative du corps électoral lui a donné quitus quant à la politique génocidaire mise en œuvre à Gaza et à l’épuration ethnique menée en Cisjordanie.

Pour autant, les 67 autres députés, représentant les oppositions, indiquent que la coalition menée par Netanyahou est rejetée par une majorité du corps électoral.

La coalition menée par Gadi Eisenkot, ancien chef de l’état-major, n’atteint pas quant à elle les objectifs qu’elle s’était fixée et n’est pas non plus en situation de former seule un gouvernement. On peut d’ailleurs constater que la plupart des sondages se sont une nouvelle fois trompés puisqu’ils plaçaient ladite coalition devant celle dirigée par Netanyahou. Au cours de la campagne, Gadi Eisenkot s’est distingué de son adversaire principal sur de nombreux sujets de politique intérieure. Ainsi, s’est-il prononcé pour la mise en place d’une commission d’enquête sur les failles sécuritaires ayant permis le 7-Octobre alors qu’elle est obstinément refusée par Netanyahou ; il s’est montré favorable à la conscription des religieux ultra-orthodoxes – les craignant-Dieu – qui y échappent depuis 1948 ; il a enfin souvent insisté sur le nécessaire respect du principe de la séparation des pouvoirs. title: Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
text: Route diversion: An election campaign poster for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with US President Donald Trump, reads in Hebrew 'We Have One Chance To Win' is seen on the back of a bus in Jerusalem. Image: UPI / Alamy StockBenjamin Netanyahu’s interest in cryptocurrency reveals both the continuing power of financial sanctions and the current limits of technological attempts to circumvent them.Thanks to the widely reported efforts of the Russian Federation, it is no longer fantasy that cryptocurrency and blockchain-based payment systems can help sanctioned actors move money, circumvent restrictions and sustain particular commercial relationships. But importantly, while crypto might facilitate payments, its use cannot replicate the broader economic benefits of access to the international financial system. Governments considering crypto as protection against financial isolation risk confusing the ability to transfer value with the ability to participate in the global economy.While Russia’s experience provides the principal case study of both the possibilities and limitations of alternative financial arrangements, the recent Israeli debate, in the days before the 27 October election, provides a particularly revealing illustration of how these considerations are spreading. Appearing on Israel’s Channel 10 TV station, Netanyahu said he was preparing for the possibility that sanctions would be applied against Israel. This is not speculation. Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient and Japan's National Police Agency form coordinated effort combining security research, threat intelligence and network expertise to identify and disrupt X.CPE botnetMOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /CNW/ -- Today, a group of private and public sector partners announced a coordinated takedown of X.CPE, a global botnet hidden in more than 1.3 million set-top boxes across more than 200 countries. Hidden on devices before they were ever sold, the botnet used subscribers' devices and home internet connections without their knowledge or consent. This takedown was led by Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security and Synthient, along with Japan's National Police Agency.

"Operations like this raise the cost for criminals and show that the infrastructure they rely on isn't out of reach," said Charley Snyder, Head of Disruption Operations at Google Threat Intelligence Group. "Disrupting X.CPE took partners across industry working together. It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries."
A familiar device hiding an unfamiliar threat
X.CPE was embedded in firmware, the software that controls a device's basic operations, before set-top boxes reached subscribers' homes. X.CPE was built to evade pre-release security checks, and Google has since updated its review process in response, as well as banned the responsible OEM and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Unlike infections that depend on a user opening a suspicious attachment or installing an application, this threat arrived as part of the device itself. Subscribers received no consent request, notification or opt-out options.Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient, working with Japan's National Police Agency, carried out a coordinated disruption campaign against X.CPE. Each organization contributed in its own way, applying its expertise in connected-device security, malware analysis, network visibility and digital fraud to analyze the botnet and disrupt its operations.Together they dismantled a threat hiding behind seemingly routine device activity: software embedded in TV set-top boxes that gave botnet controllers remote access and allowed them to exploit home broadband connections without subscriber consent. The takedown also disrupted the command-and-control domains that operate the criminal affiliates' malware modules. Russia’s own numbers on who dies in the war have been quietly disappearing from public view for more than two years.

Moscow’s state statistics office, Rosstat, has pulled dataset after dataset since the early phase of the full-scale invasion. The agency stopped publishing its annual cause-of-death breakdown in 2024, the last public tool outside analysts had used to estimate the war’s human cost, and hundreds of other Russian federal datasets have been withdrawn or stripped of substance since.

That blackout now has a direct challenger. Two hacktivist groups say they tore through Rosstat’s internal network between October 29 and November 1 and walked out with roughly 23 terabytes of data, including files they claim cover Russian military losses in Ukraine.

The Belarusian Cyber Partisans and the group known as Silent Crow jointly claimed the breach. Silent Crow said it had taken control of around 25,000 computers across Rosstat’s central office, regional branches and the Main Interregional Center for the Processing and Dissemination of Statistical Information, according to Ukrinform. A Belarusian-language line was left on compromised Rosstat pages: “No one will escape responsibility,” the Ukrainian outlet LB.ua reported.

Rosstat denies any leak

The agency confirmed its resources were attacked but rejected the scope. Rosstat said its monitoring systems picked up suspicious activity in time for staff to intervene, and that no databases or legally protected information were exposed, as reported by the South Korean outlet EconoTimes. The main Rosstat website remained unreachable when the first reports went out.

The hackers’ numbers remain their own. The two groups also diverged on volume. Cyber Partisans put the haul at more than 10 TB, while Silent Crow put it at about 23 TB, cybersecurity firm Brandefense noted, and neither group has yet released specific Russian casualty figures from the trove.

A track record of landed claims

Both groups have claimed earlier breaches that proved harder to dismiss than Russian officials first wanted. They jointly claimed the Aeroflot IT attack in July 2025, which Russian prosecutors confirmed and over which they opened a criminal investigation, Brandefense noted in the same analysis. Silent Crow earlier claimed a January 2025 breach of Russia’s property register Rosreestr, where journalists verified sample entries despite official denials.

Rosstat was once the main public source behind independent excess-mortality analyses of the war. Russian Life, citing Rosstat’s own records, reports that the agency has since stopped providing mortality data on request and that 385 federal datasets were pulled in 2024 alone.

The groups have not yet published the stolen material. Rosstat’s main website was still down when the first wave of reports went out on November 1.

Polymarket says it is returning $3.9 million to traders following last week’s supply chain attack. Website performance monitoring firm DebugBear, meanwhile, has disclosed that its DNS records were compromised.

On October 29, the prediction market halted trading on its international platform after users reported unauthorized withdrawals. Hudson Rock researchers linked the activity to malicious JavaScript served from a DebugBear address that Polymarket’s site loaded.

The script targeted logged-in traders. It checked their portfolios, and then either dumped positions or shifted assets to a wallet chosen by the attacker. The code read credential-related data stored in the browser, but Hudson Rock saw no evidence of it sending passwords, seed phrases or private keys back to the attacker. In an October 30 update, Polymarket said 726 wallets were affected. At that point, all but 37 had been made whole, and the rest were being paid once their details were checked.

DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) script lets websites measure page load performance for visitors, initially told customers to remove the embed code and has now shared its initial findings.

“Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain,” the company said.

DebugBear has not explained how the attackers obtained access at the registrar level, and its investigation is ongoing. The company said it found no indication that its internal systems were compromised.

Ransomware gang talked AI agents into doing much of its dirty work

The group behind the Aur0ra ransomware has been using AI agents to move through victim networks, collect credentials and work its way up to domain administrator access, according to Sophos.

AI-assisted intrusion workflow (Source: Sophos)

The company, which tracks the group as GOLD OGRE, recovered artifacts from the Cursor AI coding assistant in late August that show the attackers handing the agents VPN logins, proxy access, targets and objectives. The agents then mapped the network and Active Directory, hunted for passwords in network shares, documents and backups, and moved laterally with little input from the people directing them.
In some networks, the agents gained domain management access, and three of those victims were later named on Aur0ra’s data leak site. Breaking in and deploying the ransomware stayed under human control.
Prompts written in Russian
The researchers also obtained some of the operators’ instructions to the agents. In one, an operator said the Windows AD network needed testing and offered to set up a SOCKS5 proxy and user accounts for the agent.
Another instructed it, “Don’t try brute-forcing domain administrator accounts anymore. Try other, less noisy, methods and vectors.” A third asked it to find the backup servers, NAS servers and virtualization systems in the victim’s infrastructure.
Operator logs also contained keyboard slips typed in Cyrillic, which the company says suggest the operators are Russian speakers.
A red team cover story
To get around the guardrails built into the AI tools, the attackers described the intrusions as authorized red team activity or diagnostic testing. The attacks ran through Cursor’s Composer agentic coding model and models from Anthropic, xAI and Moonshot.
“Analysis indicates that the threat actors initially used Anthropic almost exclusively but then introduced other models. The shift may be related to the threat actors’ objectives, as they transitioned from building tools to conducting intrusions.,” Sophos noted.
The company’s Counter Threat Unit assesses with high confidence that GOLD OGRE used AI to test whether its tools could evade EDR products, then gave associates similar technology for Aur0ra attacks. The researchers consider it highly likely that other ransomware groups will build AI agents into their operations too.
Gambit Security and CloudSEK published their own analyses of Aur0ra operations, both apparently based on the same exposed open directory. Gambit’s report mentions a Claude 4.5-Sonnet agent being deployed in semi-automated attacks.
“AI can accelerate phases of the attack chain and reduce the level of technical aptitude needed to conduct an attack. Existing controls such as patching internet-facing devices, deploying phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), and monitoring EDR alerts are still effective, but successful defense relies on a quick response,” Sophos concluded.
